title: Arrays, memory and pointers
subtitle: Memory is a long row of numbered boxes. An array is a run of them; a pointer is a box that holds a box’s number.

sections.title: Arrays
sections.body: int a[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50}; reserves 5 consecutive ints. Indexes run 0 to 4; a[5] is out of bounds and C does not check — it silently reads or corrupts neighbouring memory. Initialise, then process with a loop.

sections.title: Addresses: memory picture
sections.body: Each byte has an address. &x is the address of x. An int array of 4 elements occupies 16 bytes; element i lives at base + 4·i. So the name a itself acts as the address of a[0].

sections.title: Pointers
sections.eyebrow: A variable that holds an address
sections.body: int *p = &x; — p stores x’s address; *p (dereference) means “the thing p points to”. *p = 9 changes x. A pointer must be initialised before use; a NULL pointer points nowhere. Pointer arithmetic scales by the element size: p + 1 moves to the next int.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Unchanged only if p were a copy.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Writing through the pointer changes x.

figures.caption: Figure 6.3.1 — Pointers
figures.note: p + 2 lands on the third element.

sections.title: Pointers and function arguments
sections.body: C passes arguments by value — a function gets copies. To let a function change the caller’s variable, pass its address: swap(&x, &y) with void swap(int *a, int *b). Arrays are passed as the address of their first element, so a function can modify them.

questions.prompt: Why can't void swap(int a, int b) swap the caller’s variables?

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Returning one value would not swap both.

figures.caption: Figure 6.4.1 — swap by pointer
figures.note: swap works on the caller’s variables through their addresses.

sections.title: Strings
sections.body: A C string is a char array ending with the null character '\0': "hi" occupies 3 bytes (h, i, \0). strlen counts up to, not including, the null. Forgetting room for the terminator is a classic overflow.

sections.title: Dynamic memory
sections.body: malloc(n) asks the heap for n bytes and returns a pointer; free(p) gives it back. Forgetting to free leaks memory; using memory after freeing (dangling pointer) or freeing twice is undefined. Pair every malloc with one free.

questions.prompt: A memory leak happens when you…

choices.text: Allocate memory and never free it.
